The city’s 53-year-old Village Halloween Parade still owns October 31st, but around it stretches a full month of costume contests, candlelit concerts, haunted pop-up bars, costume parties, and car-free streets built for trick-or-treating.
Ranging from family-friendly affairs to adult nights out, this year’s early Halloween lineup is pretty wide-ranging and already opening New Yorkers to bookmark their events.
To make your life easy, we’ve put together a list of the best Halloween events in New York for 2026 so far, and stay tuned as we continually update the list!
The NYC Village Halloween Parade
Getty Images / Stephanie Keith

New York’s biggest Halloween tradition turns 53 this year, and it’s still the same idea Greenwich Village puppeteer Ralph Lee started back in 1974: a neighborhood walk that grew into the world’s largest Halloween parade.

It takes over Sixth Avenue from Spring Street to 16th Street on Saturday, October 31st at 7 pm, drawing roughly two million spectators and thousands of costumed marchers, plus giant hand-built puppets and more than 50 marching bands.
This year’s theme is “Body & Soul,” with the full theme statement expected shortly.

Anyone can march, just show up in costume to the lineup at Canal Street and Sixth Avenue between 6:30 and 9 pm, no registration required. Spectators should grab a spot along the route by 8:30 pm, and the parade runs rain, shine, or wind.
Candlelight: Halloween Classics
Source / Fever
Candlelight’s Halloween edition takes over the Church of the Heavenly Rest, the neo-Gothic, Art Deco landmark facing Central Park that’s already one of the Upper East Side’s most overlooked gems.

The Highline String Quartet performs a full set of horror and thriller themes, Michael Jackson’s “Thriller,” John Carpenter’s “Halloween,” the “Psycho” prelude, “Ghostbusters,” “Beetlejuice,” and Saint-Saëns’ “Danse Macabre” among them, all under the glow of hundreds of candles inside a church whose stained glass usually gets all the attention.
The show runs 60 minutes, with doors opening 45 minutes early and closing five minutes before showtime, no late entry.
Tickets are open to ages 8 and up, seating is first-come, first-served within each pricing zone starting at $30!
Boo at the Zoo at Bronx Zoo
Source / Terria Clay ©WCS
Bronx Zoo (2300 Southern Blvd, The Bronx(
The Bronx Zoo‘s beloved fall festival returns across 265 acres and more than 11,000 animals, with three brand-new additions for 2026 leading the way.

The Hay Maze & Challenge Course has kids climbing, crawling, and balancing through custom straw sculptures shaped like animals, Animal Chats bring zoo experts out for live Q&As on some of the park’s most fascinating species, and the new Boo Carnival rolls out classic games like Pumpkin Smash and ring toss.

Signature traditions return too: a stilt-walker costume parade followed by a Boo Dance Party, the Pumpkin Garden’s giant animal-shaped pumpkin displays, a Wildlife Theater puppet show, free face painting, and an Extinct Animal Species Graveyard that turns conservation into a spooky lesson.
Boo at the Zoo is included with regular zoo admission and free for WCS members, but reservations are required and tend to sell out fast.
Tickets aren’t timed this year, giving visitors flexibility to explore at their own pace, and are available now at BronxZoo.com/Boo.
The Great Jack O’Lantern Blaze
Photo courtesy of Jack O’Lantern Blaze / Tom Nycz
Van Cortlandt Manor, Corton-on-Hudson, NY

The Great Jack O’Lantern Blaze is one of the most stunning visual Halloween experiences that returns each fall, featuring 7,000+ uniquely carved pumpkins forming larger-than-life glowing art installations. From returning fan favorites like the Sea Serpent, the Pumpkin Planetarium, and a spinning pumpkin carousel, there are endless surreal displays to explore along the path.

New for 2026, visitors can explore the event’s longest pumpkin trail in history—featuring selfie photo ops with carved movie monsters in the Creature Feature Forest, glowing fable scenes on Literary Lane, an interactive lawn dance party at the manor house, and quick-sip stops at the new Creature’s Cantina popup. Located just an hour from NYC in Hudson Valley at Van Cortlandt Manor in Croton-on-Hudson, the 2026 spectacle kicks off on September 18 and runs for 44 select nights through November 8. Tickets and more info here.
Halloween Harvest Festival at Socrates Sculpture Park
Source / Socrates Sculpture Park
Socrates Sculpture Park
This free, family-friendly festival doubles as Socrates Sculpture Park’s season finale, landing right on Halloween day this year along the East River waterfront in Long Island City.

It’s built around New York’s second-largest dog costume contest, co-presented with Chateau le Woof, where registration opens on-site around 1 pm and the contest itself typically kicks off mid-afternoon with prizes for the winner, runner-up, and third place.

Beyond the dog contest, the day usually blends hands-on fall activities with community programming: past editions have included drop-in pumpkin decorating and carving contests, costume-making workshops using reused materials, a community resource fair, live harvest-themed performances, and even a pumpkin catapult one year that launched leftover gourds into the park’s compost pile.
The park’s Saturday farmstand also typically runs earlier in the day for anyone wanting to grab produce before the festivities start.
The organizers note that the full 2026 lineup and schedule are still being finalized, so specifics like this year’s workshop list and any special performers haven’t been announced yet.
It’s free with RSVP recommended, and details will be posted as they’re confirmed on Socrates Sculpture Park’s event page.
Trick or Streets
Source / NYC DOT

Trick-or-Streets is NYC Department of Transportation’s month-long Halloween initiative that shuts down Open Streets, pedestrian plazas, and select corridors to car traffic across all five boroughs, turning them into car-free spaces for trick-or-treating, live music, interactive performances, and harvest-themed activities.

It launched in 2022 specifically to address child pedestrian safety on Halloween, historically one of the most dangerous nights of the year for kids on foot, and it has grown every year since, reaching a record 137 street closures across the five boroughs in 2025.

New for 2026, partner organizations can host neighborhood walking tours spotlighting local culture and history as part of their programming, in addition to the usual mix of parades, block parties, and costume contests. A few flagship corridors are already locked in, including Castleton Avenue in Staten Island, Vernon Boulevard in Queens, St. Nicholas Avenue in Manhattan, and 61st Street in Queens, with dozens more expected to join as the application window closes.

Expect the full event map and schedule, likely covering mid-October through October 31, to be announced by NYC DOT sometime in early-to-mid October. The most current info will be posted at nyc.gov/trickorstreet
Mind of a Serial Killer: The Experience
Source / Mind of a Serial Killer: The Experience
This is less a Halloween pop-up than a genuine true-crime museum, and it’s now settled into a 24,500-square-foot former retail space at the corner of 14th Street and Sixth Avenue for an extended run.

Across more than 20 immersive stops, the exhibition recreates real crime scenes tied to 20 of history’s most notorious killers, including Ted Bundy’s Beetle and Jeffrey Dahmer’s apartment, alongside evidence, forensic timelines tracing serial crime back to the early 1900s, and a VR segment that drops visitors directly into an investigation.

The full visit runs 90 to 120 minutes, and this one comes with real content warnings: it contains graphic material related to victims of all ages, a digital waiver is required before entry, and the age policy is 14+, with anyone under 17 needing an adult.
Tickets are available now!
Black Lagoon Pop-Up Bar
Source / Black Lagoon
Someday Bar – 364 Atlantic Ave, Brooklyn

Every fall, the cozy, brick-walled Someday Bar in Boerum Hill trades its usual identity for a full submersion into Black Lagoon, the award-winning traveling Halloween pop-up created by industry veterans Erin Hayes and Kelsey Ramage.

This year it’s part of a 34-bar takeover spanning the US and Canada, transforming acclaimed cocktail spots, including several James Beard-recognized and Tales of the Cocktail Spirited Award-winning bars, into immersive haunted lounges with cinematic lighting, eerie soundscapes, and an entirely new seasonal cocktail menu.

Past years have turned the space into a kraken-topped, upside-down-style haunted realm, and while the full 2026 menu hasn’t dropped yet, early teasers point to drinks like Abyssa’s Obsession, a pumpkin-spiced riff on a piña colada made with Kraken rum and Lustau sherry, Bone Temple, a fall-inspired margarita with tequila and spiced oat orgeat, and Moon Shadow, a nutmeg-and-cold-brew twist on an espresso martini. Guests can also pick up limited-edition glassware, including a new Abyssa the Octo-Witch tiki mug made in collaboration with Tiki Farm.

Reservations are recommended for parties of six or more, while smaller groups are first-come, first-served, and last year’s Brooklyn run stretched from October 1 through November 2, so expect a similar multi-week window this year.
More information soon about the full menu and string of dates.
Circoloco New York Halloween 2026
Source / Chris Lavado, Off Brand Project
Brooklyn Storehouse

The Ibiza-born party institution returns to Brooklyn for its annual Halloween takeover, and this year comes with an ending built in: it’s the final Circoloco event at Brooklyn Storehouse, making this the last chance to catch the party there.
Organizers expanded the usual two-night format into a full three-day run, going through Sunday.
The lineup is stacked with house and techno heavyweights, including Seth Troxler, Dixon, ANOTR, Carlita, Rampa, &ME, Beltran, and Jimi Jules, and so many more.
Tickets are sold out and waitlisted for both Friday and Saturday, but limited Sunday passes remain! Shop all of the dates here.
Halloween bars in NYC
Source / Loreley Beer Garden
Put your spirit to the test at one of NYC’s ghoulish bars before Halloween night.
Treat yourself to a seasonal cocktail at a bar or speakeasy that gives off the spook-tacular vibes you’re after!
Check out our guide to the best spooky bars and restaurants in NYC for Halloween vibes and stay tuned for more that get announced in the coming weeks.
Autumn Glow Festival in New Rochelle, NY
Source / Westchester County Tourism & Autumn Glow Festival

This lantern walk lights up Glen Island Park, a 105-acre stretch of New Rochelle that has a wilder backstory than most people realize: it’s widely considered the site of America’s first theme park, built in 1881 by a shipping magnate who linked five islands together with pagodas, a German castle, and even a small zoo, decades before Disneyland existed.

Now the same grounds host over 1,000 hand-crafted lanterns inspired by traditional Chinese lantern-making, strung along an illuminated walking trail with tunnels, larger-than-life LED sculptures, and food trucks scattered throughout.
The full walk takes about an hour and is best experienced after sunset when the lanterns really pop, and it’s designed as a rain-or-shine event with built-in rescheduling for extreme weather.
Tickets start at $17.84 and it’s roughly a 30-45 minute trip from Manhattan by car or a quick Metro-North ride from Grand Central to New Rochelle.
Halloween Extravaganza at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine
Source / Maike Schulz for Cathedral St. John the Divine
The Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine (1047 Amsterdam Ave)
Few Halloween traditions in the city pair genuine artistry with genuine scares quite like this one.

Set inside the world’s largest Gothic cathedral, the evening opens with a screening of the 1920s silent horror classic Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, accompanied live by world-renowned organist David Briggs on the Cathedral’s monumental Aeolian-Skinner pipe organ, an instrument so powerful it can shake the stone beneath your feet. Briggs is a fixture of the Cathedral’s music program, known for his own organ transcriptions of major orchestral works, and pairing his playing with a silent film is a rare treat even by St. John the Divine’s standards.

The night’s signature moment comes after the film, when a procession of “Ghouls and Ghosts” winds through the audience, a callback to the Cathedral’s longtime Procession of the Ghouls tradition, which in past years has featured performers from the Mettawee River Theater Company emerging in costume to startle and delight the crowd. It’s a genuinely unique blend of horror-movie history, world-class organ music, and theatrical spectacle inside one of Manhattan’s most awe-inspiring interiors.
Tickets run on tiered pricing this year at $50 and $75, the event is recommended for ages 8 and up, and past editions have sold out well in advance, so early booking is worth it.
Tickets and updates are available through the Cathedral’s official calendar
Halloween at Rooftop Cinema Club Midtown
Add caption
1441 Broadway

Rooftop Cinema Club’s Midtown terrace turns its month-long “Fright Club” programming into one of the city’s most atmospheric ways to watch horror movies, with the Empire State Building lit up just blocks south of the screen.

Every seat comes with wireless headphones that block out traffic three floors below, so the soundtrack stays crisp whether you’re in a single Adirondack chair or a two-person loveseat, and a full craft bar serves cocktails, local beer, and wine a few steps from the back row.

October’s lineup covers the full spectrum of horror fandom. Dog owners can bring their pups to Wooftop-friendly screenings of The Sheep Detectives and Hocus Pocus, families get daytime hits like Minions & Monsters, Halloweentown, and The Addams Family (1991), and a Supernatural TV marathon rounds out the lighter fare.

For genuine scares, the schedule runs from newer releases like Weapons and Backrooms through cult staples such as Practical Magic, The Rocky Horror Picture Show, and Edward Scissorhands, all the way to genre-defining classics including Rosemary’s Baby, The Exorcist (1973), The Evil Dead (1981), and Psycho (1960), plus modern thrillers like American Psycho, The Silence of the Lambs, Twin Peaks, and Get Out.
Tickets start around $12.50 and climb to roughly $36 depending on seat type and showtime, available now through Rooftop Cinema Club.
Pumpkin Smash at Hudson River Park
Source / Jay Belsky & Hudson River Park
Pier 84 – Hudson River Park

This is Hudson River Park’s annual answer to the post-Halloween pumpkin graveyard: bring an old jack-o’-lantern or uncarved gourd to Pier 84, grab a bat, hammer, or shovel, and smash it into compostable scraps that get repurposed to enrich soil throughout the park’s four-mile footprint.

It’s become a genuinely fun family tradition since launching years ago, with past editions adding free face painting and circus performances from Bindlestiff Family Cirkus on top of the smashing itself.
The event is completely free and open to all ages, no registration required, just show up with a pumpkin in hand.

Beyond the one-day event, Hudson River Park also runs 10 year-round compost drop-off sites across the park, including one at Pier 84 itself, for anyone who wants to keep the sustainability streak going past Halloween weekend.
Edgar Allan Poe Speakeasy in Peekskill, NY
Edgar Allan Poe Speakeasy: Chapter Two
This touring immersive-theater experience, produced by Midnight Creative, turns Peekskill’s Dramatic Hall into a gothic cocktail den built entirely around Edgar Allan Poe.

Over 90 minutes, “Poe Historians” walk guests through four of his most famous tales, The Tell-Tale Heart, The Black Cat, The Raven, and The Masque of the Red Death, with a themed cocktail paired to each story: the Pale Blue Eye, The Cat’s Meow, Nevermore, and the Cocktail of the Red Death.
It leans more toward dramatic storytelling and craft cocktails than jump scares, making it a solid pick for a date night or a group looking for something atmospheric rather than a haunted house.
It’s a 21-and-up event with valid ID required, though zero-proof mocktail pairings are available for anyone skipping alcohol.
Trick-or treating around NYC
Shutterstock / Brian Goodman
Get out your candy buckets and figure out your trick or treating route because collecting goodies in NYC is truly unmatched!
No matter what borough you’re in, nothing beats going door to door for some sweet treats.
Check out our guide on the best neighborhoods to going trick or treating in NYC each year.
Haunted houses in and near NYC
Source / Blood Manor
Get ready for a spine-chilling adventure as you visit some of the most terrifying haunted houses in and around NYC this Halloween season.

From the eerie Blood Manor which features 10,000 square feet of terrifying rooms, narrow halls, and hidden passageways to the immersive Ridgewood Asylum with the most terrifying escape rooms in the city, there’s plenty of places to let out some screams and feel your bones chill.
Pumpkin picking in NYC and beyond
Pexels via James Wheeler
Spooky season is right around the corner, and there’s no better way to celebrate than by visiting the top pumpkin picking spots in NYC and its surroundings!
Whether you’re decorating your home with a cute or creepy gourd, or looking to enjoy a day out, these locations offer a variety of pumpkins, Instagrammable moments, and more.
Don’t miss out on the full list of must-visit pumpkin patches, including options for apple orchards and corn mazes to complete your fall adventure.
Halloween decorations in NYC neighborhoods
Instagram / @nyclovesnyc
While still a bit aways still, you know New Yorkers always go all out when pulling out their Halloween decorations!

From the haunted Greenwich Village to the residential Upper East Side, there are tons of neighborhoods to walk through and admire their spookiness. This is one of our favorite free ways to spend a few hours getting into the Halloween spirit!
Check out our favorite neighborhoods for decorations here!
Where: All around NYC
The Penny Williamsburg’s Yappy Hour
Source / The Penny Williamsburg
The Halloween costume competition has some very cute new contenders!
On October 25, The Penny Williamsburg is teaming up with Brooklyn nonprofit Badass Animal Rescue for an afternoon of adoptable dogs dressed in their spooky-season best.

Meet the pups from noon to 2 pm, then head upstairs to elNico, the hotel’s Mexican rooftop restaurant and bar, for Yappy Hour from 1 to 4 pm. You can sip cocktails with skyline views while supporting the rescue, with $1 from every signature cocktail donated to help dogs find loving homes!
Costumes are encouraged, so give your Halloween outfit an early outing. You might even meet your future four-legged roommate!
Halloween Spooktacular at Hudson Yards
Source / Hudson Yards
Hudson Yards is giving the kids somewhere to burn off that Halloween excitement before the evening candy haul.
Its Fall Spooktacular takes over the Public Square and Gardens on October 31, with a free afternoon of live music, dancing, and costume-ready photo ops.
The fun starts at 11 am with Mozart for Munchkins’ Halloween-themed concert, before DJ KB takes over at 1 pm for a KIDZ BOP Monster Bash Dance Party packed with kid-friendly Halloween singalongs.

Want to keep the festivities going? Vessel ticket holders can also go trick-or-treating inside the landmark, decorate pumpkins, and have a robot turn their photo into a Halloween caricature. Those extras require a separate Vessel ticket, while the outdoor celebration is free with an RSVP available on the event page. Costumes are encouraged!
More details here!
Barktoberfest at Pier 57
Add caption
Your dog’s Halloween costume deserves more than a quick lap around the block!

On October 17, Pier 57 and DOWNTOWN Magazine are bringing Barktoberfest back to the pier’s nearly two-acre Rooftop Park for a free celebration of pups, pet parents, and wonderfully over-the-top outfits.

Check-in begins at 11 am, with the dog costume contest kicking off at noon. Pet parents can register their pups for a chance to win prizes, while spectators can simply show up and enjoy the adorable competition with the Hudson River and Lower Manhattan as the backdrop.

After the contest, head downstairs to Market 57 for lunch, or grab bites for purchase from Al Volo on the rooftop. Bird & Branch will also serve dog treats, so the four-legged guests won’t miss out on the snacks!
More details here!
Tompkins Square Halloween Dog Parade
Shutterstock / Gordon Donovan
The cutest fall event in NYC — thousands of costumed dogs will take over Avenue B!

If you want a Halloween outing that’s more “aww” than “boo,” the 36th annual Tompkins Square Halloween Dog Parade returns to the East Village on Saturday, October 17, 2026, featuring an elaborate costume competition, sponsor activations, live broadcast, and adoptable rescue spotlighting.
Registration for the costume competition can be done at NYDogParade.org.
Head to Blue Point Brewing for costume parties, cash prizes, and Halloween brews
Source / Blue Point Brewing

Blue Point Brewing is giving you three chances to take your Halloween costume out for a spin in Patchogue, with a Rocky Horror-themed party, a late-night reggaeton bash, and a Halloween-night celebration with cash prizes.

First up is the Halloween Horror Show on October 23, inspired by The Rocky Horror Picture Show. Doors open at 6 p.m., and $25 tickets include your first drink, a limited-edition pint glass, and entry into the costume contest. This one is 21+ only, and pets will need to sit it out.
On October 30, Spooky Brewery brings reggaeton to the brewery for the first time, with doors opening at 10 p.m., tickets priced at $10–$20, and a $1,000 costume prize up for grabs.

Then, on October 31, Boo-dy Barn rounds out the festivities with a DJ, beer specials, and prizes of $500 for the best group costume and $250 for the best individual costume. The $20 ticket includes your first beer and optional costume contest entry.
And here’s a particularly good reason to coordinate outfits: anyone dressed as a hot dog or condiment gets a free hot dog!

Autumn Glow Festival in New Rochelle, NY

Source / Westchester County Tourism & Autumn Glow Festival

This lantern walk lights up Glen Island Park, a 105-acre stretch of New Rochelle that has a wilder backstory than most people realize: it’s widely considered the site of America’s first theme park, built in 1881 by a shipping magnate who linked five islands together with pagodas, a German castle, and even a small zoo, decades before Disneyland existed.


Now the same grounds host over 1,000 hand-crafted lanterns inspired by traditional Chinese lantern-making, strung along an illuminated walking trail with tunnels, larger-than-life LED sculptures, and food trucks scattered throughout.


The full walk takes about an hour and is best experienced after sunset when the lanterns really pop, and it’s designed as a rain-or-shine event with built-in rescheduling for extreme weather.


Tickets start at $17.84 and it’s roughly a 30-45 minute trip from Manhattan by car or a quick Metro-North ride from Grand Central to New Rochelle.

Halloween Extravaganza at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine

Source / Maike Schulz for Cathedral St. John the Divine

The Cathedral Church of St. John the Divine (1047 Amsterdam Ave)

Few Halloween traditions in the city pair genuine artistry with genuine scares quite like this one.


Set inside the world’s largest Gothic cathedral, the evening opens with a screening of the 1920s silent horror classic Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, accompanied live by world-renowned organist David Briggs on the Cathedral’s monumental Aeolian-Skinner pipe organ, an instrument so powerful it can shake the stone beneath your feet. Briggs is a fixture of the Cathedral’s music program, known for his own organ transcriptions of major orchestral works, and pairing his playing with a silent film is a rare treat even by St. John the Divine’s standards.


The night’s signature moment comes after the film, when a procession of “Ghouls and Ghosts” winds through the audience, a callback to the Cathedral’s longtime Procession of the Ghouls tradition, which in past years has featured performers from the Mettawee River Theater Company emerging in costume to startle and delight the crowd. It’s a genuinely unique blend of horror-movie history, world-class organ music, and theatrical spectacle inside one of Manhattan’s most awe-inspiring interiors.


Tickets run on tiered pricing this year at $50 and $75, the event is recommended for ages 8 and up, and past editions have sold out well in advance, so early booking is worth it.


Tickets and updates are available through the Cathedral’s official calendar

Halloween at Rooftop Cinema Club Midtown

Add caption

1441 Broadway

Rooftop Cinema Club’s Midtown terrace turns its month-long “Fright Club” programming into one of the city’s most atmospheric ways to watch horror movies, with the Empire State Building lit up just blocks south of the screen.


Every seat comes with wireless headphones that block out traffic three floors below, so the soundtrack stays crisp whether you’re in a single Adirondack chair or a two-person loveseat, and a full craft bar serves cocktails, local beer, and wine a few steps from the back row.


October’s lineup covers the full spectrum of horror fandom. Dog owners can bring their pups to Wooftop-friendly screenings of The Sheep Detectives and Hocus Pocus, families get daytime hits like Minions & Monsters, Halloweentown, and The Addams Family (1991), and a Supernatural TV marathon rounds out the lighter fare.


For genuine scares, the schedule runs from newer releases like Weapons and Backrooms through cult staples such as Practical Magic, The Rocky Horror Picture Show, and Edward Scissorhands, all the way to genre-defining classics including Rosemary’s Baby, The Exorcist (1973), The Evil Dead (1981), and Psycho (1960), plus modern thrillers like American Psycho, The Silence of the Lambs, Twin Peaks, and Get Out.


Tickets start around $12.50 and climb to roughly $36 depending on seat type and showtime, available now through Rooftop Cinema Club.

Pumpkin Smash at Hudson River Park

Source / Jay Belsky & Hudson River Park

Pier 84 – Hudson River Park

This is Hudson River Park’s annual answer to the post-Halloween pumpkin graveyard: bring an old jack-o’-lantern or uncarved gourd to Pier 84, grab a bat, hammer, or shovel, and smash it into compostable scraps that get repurposed to enrich soil throughout the park’s four-mile footprint.


It’s become a genuinely fun family tradition since launching years ago, with past editions adding free face painting and circus performances from Bindlestiff Family Cirkus on top of the smashing itself.


The event is completely free and open to all ages, no registration required, just show up with a pumpkin in hand.


Beyond the one-day event, Hudson River Park also runs 10 year-round compost drop-off sites across the park, including one at Pier 84 itself, for anyone who wants to keep the sustainability streak going past Halloween weekend.

Edgar Allan Poe Speakeasy in Peekskill, NY

Edgar Allan Poe Speakeasy: Chapter Two

This touring immersive-theater experience, produced by Midnight Creative, turns Peekskill’s Dramatic Hall into a gothic cocktail den built entirely around Edgar Allan Poe.


Over 90 minutes, “Poe Historians” walk guests through four of his most famous tales, The Tell-Tale Heart, The Black Cat, The Raven, and The Masque of the Red Death, with a themed cocktail paired to each story: the Pale Blue Eye, The Cat’s Meow, Nevermore, and the Cocktail of the Red Death.


It leans more toward dramatic storytelling and craft cocktails than jump scares, making it a solid pick for a date night or a group looking for something atmospheric rather than a haunted house.


It’s a 21-and-up event with valid ID required, though zero-proof mocktail pairings are available for anyone skipping alcohol.

The Penny Williamsburg’s Yappy Hour

Source / The Penny Williamsburg

The Halloween costume competition has some very cute new contenders!

Head to Blue Point Brewing for costume parties, cash prizes, and Halloween brews

Source / Blue Point Brewing

Blue Point Brewing is giving you three chances to take your Halloween costume out for a spin in Patchogue, with a Rocky Horror-themed party, a late-night reggaeton bash, and a Halloween-night celebration with cash prizes.


First up is the Halloween Horror Show on October 23, inspired by The Rocky Horror Picture Show. Doors open at 6 p.m., and $25 tickets include your first drink, a limited-edition pint glass, and entry into the costume contest. This one is 21+ only, and pets will need to sit it out.


On October 30, Spooky Brewery brings reggaeton to the brewery for the first time, with doors opening at 10 p.m., tickets priced at $10–$20, and a $1,000 costume prize up for grabs.


Then, on October 31, Boo-dy Barn rounds out the festivities with a DJ, beer specials, and prizes of $500 for the best group costume and $250 for the best individual costume. The $20 ticket includes your first beer and optional costume contest entry.
